period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 8 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 6h 0min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading activation: sorting wonders and nature's power (p.137)

time_bands.activity: Display the pictures from the textbook on the board and invite students to sort them into natural and man-made wonders in pairs. Take brief share-outs and note categories on the board.
Open the discussion to the whole class: which kind of wonder is more appealing and why? Encourage students to give reasons; record key descriptive words they use.
Read aloud the opening paragraphs of 'Spectacular Wonders' (p.137–139) with students following in their textbooks, pausing to point out the seven phenomena listed.
Continue shared reading through to the Lonar Crater Lake section (p.139–141), modelling how to identify the location, special feature, and descriptive language for each wonder.

In groups of four, students begin the web-chart task — jotting words they associate with 'Nature's Power' drawn from the sections just read. Groups share two or three words aloud before the class closes.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening encounter with the text works best when students notice that the text moves from broad claim to individual profile — draw attention to that structure during shared reading. A common difficulty is distinguishing the seven phenomena by location; writing each name and state on the board as it appears in the reading gives students an anchor. The two remaining pre-reading activities (discussing personal wonders and completing the web chart fully) may be taken up as independent exploration.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Remaining Wonders and Mapping the Seven

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — complete the table of seven phenomena, location, and unique feature (p.142)

time_bands.activity: Continue guided reading of the text from Magnetic Hills through to Chandipur Beach (p.141–142), with students tracking location and one unique feature for each wonder as they read.
Read aloud the concluding paragraph that frames the phenomena as a blend of science and folklore. Discuss briefly: what does the writer mean by 'extraordinary forces shaping our environment'?
Students work individually to complete the information table (p.142) for all seven phenomena. After a suitable interval, pairs compare entries and reconcile any differences by returning to the text.
Whole-class check: call on different students for each row of the table and confirm answers. Address any confusion about the Sundarbans and Bioluminescence entries, which students often conflate.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full text, students now consolidate it into the table — the act of completing the table is itself a re-reading task, so allow them to scan freely. A frequent error is writing the state instead of the specific district for location; remind students the table asks for the district where given. The writing-based self-extension task (student's personal favourite wonder) is available as independent exploration for those who finish early.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading of Extracts and Authorial Choices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — Extract 1: figurative language and author's opening statement (p.142–143)
Let us think and reflect — Extract 2: Chandipur Beach, rhetorical question and purpose (p.143–144)

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss — answer questions on Living Root Bridges and Lonar Crater Lake (p.144)

time_bands.activity: Read Extract 1 aloud ('India is home to some of the most mystifying natural phenomena…', p.142). Ask students what the phrase 'spark our imagination' does to the reader — brief think-pair-share.

Students work through the four sub-questions for Extract 1 (p.142–143) individually, then discuss answers as a class. Focus the discussion on how replacing 'home to' with a phrase from the extract sharpens the analysis.
Read Extract 2 aloud ('Have you seen things disappearing in front of your eyes?…', p.143). Ask: why does a writer open with a question? Collect responses and list the purposes students suggest.
Students answer the four sub-questions for Extract 2 (p.143–144) individually. Review the assertion-reason question as a class, walking through the logic of each option.
Set the homework task: students read the two short-answer questions about the Living Root Bridges and Lonar Crater Lake (p.144) and write their answers before the next encounter with the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: Having mapped all seven phenomena into the table, students are now ready to move from recall to analysis — the key shift in critical reading is asking not just what the text says but what the writer chose to do and why. The assertion-reason format is unfamiliar to many Grade VIII students; slow down on that item and model how to test each part independently before combining them. The ECR and personal-response questions (what the writer's purpose might be; which wonder the student found most interesting) are rich but time-consuming and are better suited to individual written exploration outside class.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Natural Phenomenon and Presenting a Place

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — mark four true statements from a sibling conversation about Rainbow Mountain (p.148)
Let us speak — group presentation on a place of interest in your region (p.148)

time_bands.activity: Orient students: they will hear a brother and sister discussing the Rainbow Mountain of Peru. Ask them to read through the six statements (p.148) silently before listening begins.
Read the transcript aloud at a measured pace. Students mark each statement true or false as they listen. Read it a second time to allow students to check or revise their markings.
Discuss the answers as a class, asking students to explain what in the conversation led them to mark each statement. Emphasise that statements 1 and 5 are the ones most students mark incorrectly.

Introduce the group presentation task (p.148): groups of four choose a place of interest in their region and plan across the ten slides outlined in the guidelines. Groups discuss and divide responsibilities.
Each group gives a brief rehearsal presentation (two to three minutes each, where time allows). Peers offer one piece of positive feedback and one suggestion after each group; teacher facilitates.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored how the text profiles each Indian wonder, the listening task extends that attention to a global natural phenomenon — draw students' notice to the similar structure: location, formation, and distinctive quality. For the speaking task, groups benefit from the slide guidelines as a scaffold; circulate during planning to ensure groups have a specific place in mind and are not choosing something too generic. Groups that do not present fully in this encounter may complete their presentations as a spoken-language activity in their own time.

periods.activity_title: Planning and Drafting a Descriptive Essay

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — descriptive essay for school magazine on a natural object, place or event (p.148)

time_bands.activity: Discuss what makes the text's descriptions of the seven wonders vivid — draw out use of precise location, sensory detail, and figurative language. Explain that students will write their own descriptive essay using similar techniques.
Walk students through the format: title, introduction, two or three body paragraphs, conclusion. Show a brief model structure on the board and annotate what each part does.

Students individually choose their subject (a natural object, place, or event they have experienced) and complete a planning grid: subject, title, one-sentence introduction idea, two or three body points, one-sentence conclusion idea.
Students write their full draft — introduction and body paragraphs — in their exercise books. Teacher circulates, giving brief individual feedback on descriptive language and paragraph structure.
Students write their conclusion paragraph and read through their complete draft. Pairs swap drafts and offer one written comment about the most effective descriptive detail their partner used.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read how the informational text profiles each wonder with precise sensory and factual language, students now attempt that descriptive register in their own voice — a natural bridge from reading to writing. A common difficulty at this stage is writing too generally ('it was beautiful'); prompt students to name specific details (colour, sound, movement, scale) the way the text names specific features of each wonder. Each student's essay is planned, drafted, peer-read, and closed within this encounter — no continuation is assumed.

periods.activity_title: Expressions, Synonyms, and Binomials from the Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — fill blanks with six expressions from the text box (p.144)
Let us learn — match five words to synonyms from the box using a thesaurus (p.145)
Let us learn — match eight binomials to their meanings in Column 2 (p.145)

time_bands.activity: Write the six expressions on the board: came into existence / to no end / in full glory / in disbelief / to name a few / age-old problem. Students predict meanings from context before filling the six blanks (p.144). Review answers together.

Students use a thesaurus to match the five words to their synonyms from the box (p.145): exotic, colossal, spectacular, serene, enigmatic. Brief whole-class check focusing on how each word appeared in the text.

Introduce binomials: explain the fixed-pair structure with two or three quick examples from everyday language. Students match the eight binomials to their meanings (p.145) individually, then compare with a partner.
Whole-class review of the binomial matching. For two or three binomials, invite students to use them in spoken sentences about the chapter's natural wonders — reinforcing meaning through context.

periods.teacher_notes: The expressions and synonyms in this encounter are drawn directly from the 'Spectacular Wonders' text, so return to the passage whenever a word's meaning is contested — contextual verification is more durable than dictionary definition alone. Binomials are a distinctive feature students encounter in the text ('part and parcel', 'leaps and bounds') and often under-notice; naming them as a grammatical category builds metalinguistic awareness. The sentence-writing extension for binomials is available as self-directed vocabulary practice.

periods.activity_title: Participles and Gerunds: Form, Function, and Practice

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — fill blanks with present or past participle form of given verbs (p.146)
Let us learn — underline and label gerunds (G) and participles (P) in sentences (p.147)
Let us learn — combine sentence pairs using participles or gerunds (p.148)

time_bands.activity: Write the highlighted words from the text on the board — living, striking, rugged, Crossing. Ask students to say what part of speech each seems to be, and how they know. Establish the distinction: participle (adjective function) vs gerund (noun function).

Students fill the five blanks using the correct participle form of the verbs in the box (p.146): stand, amaze, carve, scatter. Review answers, identifying whether each is a present or past participle and what noun it modifies.

Students read the seven sentences (p.147), underline gerunds and participles, and write G or P beside each. Class discussion focuses on how the same -ing form can be a noun in one sentence and an adjective in another.

Students combine the four sentence pairs using the specified form — participle or gerund (p.148). Two or three responses are shared aloud and class agrees on whether the combination is grammatically accurate and natural.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with contextual vocabulary in the previous encounter, the grammar focus now shifts to how verb forms function as other parts of speech — a conceptual step up that needs concrete examples from the text itself. The most persistent confusion is between gerunds and present participles, since both end in -ing; anchor the distinction by returning to the text examples (Crossing as subject = gerund; living bridges = participle). Any student who finishes the sentence-combination task early may write two original sentences using a gerund and a participle drawn from the wonders described in the text.

periods.activity_title: Synthesis: India's Wonders — Man-Made, Natural, and Bioluminescent

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore — research and discuss man-made wonders: Kallanai Dam, Nalanda, Hampi, modern feats (p.154)
Let us explore — identify the bioluminescent insect and connect it to the Glowing Waters phenomenon (p.154)

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief whole-class recall: students name as many of the seven natural wonders from the text as they can, along with one unique feature each. Record responses on the board to create a collective map of what the chapter covered.

Introduce the four man-made wonders: Kallanai Dam, Nalanda, Hampi's musical pillars, and modern engineering feats such as the Bandra-Worli Sea Link and the Statue of Unity. Students read the brief descriptions (p.154) and discuss in pairs: what makes these man-made wonders comparable to the natural ones described in the text?

Revisit the concept of bioluminescence from the Glowing Waters of Kerala section of the text. Students study the image of the bioluminescent insect (p.154), identify it, and discuss: what other life forms share this quality? Students record the insect's name in their own regional language if they know it.

Groups of four choose one natural wonder from the text and one man-made wonder from today's reading and prepare a two-minute spoken comparison: what human need or environmental force created each, and what makes both worth knowing about?

Two or three groups share their comparisons. Close with a whole-class reflection: across all the wonders — natural and man-made — what single idea about India's landscape and human ingenuity stands out most to the class?

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis encounter draws on the full chapter — the seven natural phenomena profiled in the text, the grammar of descriptive language, and the descriptive essay students wrote — to position India's wonders within a broader interdisciplinary frame of science, history, and culture. Students may not have visited any of these sites; the comparison task works through the language and ideas of the text itself. Encourage students who know local names for the firefly or other bioluminescent organisms to share them — this connects the national wonders to their immediate environment.
materials: Atlas or printed map of India (optional)

items.source_lo: Student activates prior knowledge and identifies key information from an informational text using informational reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Pre-reading activation around seven natural wonders of India; web chart on Nature's Power.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about natural wonders of India. Mark each statement True or False.
1. The Valley of Flowers is located in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand.
2. Bioluminescence in Kumbalangi village is caused by a high concentration of macro-planktons.
3. The Sundarbans is home to Bengal tigers, estuarine crocodiles, and Indian pythons.
4. Chandipur Beach is located in the Buldhana district.

options.text: Bioluminescence in Kumbalangi village is caused by a high concentration of macro-planktons.
Chandipur Beach is located in the Buldhana district.
The Sundarbans is home to Bengal tigers, estuarine crocodiles, and Indian pythons.
The Valley of Flowers is located in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the text places the Valley of Flowers in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand.
2. False — the text states micro-planktons (not macro-planktons) cause the bioluminescence.
3. True — the text names all three animals as inhabitants of the Sundarbans.
4. False — Chandipur Beach is in Balasore district, Odisha; Buldhana is the location of Lonar Crater Lake.

items.item_stem: The text 'Spectacular Wonders' profiles seven natural phenomena of India. Choose any two phenomena from different regions of India and explain in two to three sentences what makes each one a 'wonder of nature.' Use specific details from the text.

expected_elements: Names two phenomena from different Indian regions.
States one specific unique feature for each phenomenon.
Uses a detail from the text, not a general observation.
Response is two to three sentences, clearly organised.

items.source_context: Seven natural phenomena — Valley of Flowers, Living Root Bridges, Lonar Crater Lake, Magnetic Hills, Glowing Waters, Sundarbans, Chandipur Beach — with location and unique features.
items.item_stem: The text describes the Magnetic Hills near Leh, Ladakh as an optical illusion. What causes this illusion, and why might it be misleading to visitors who do not know the explanation? Answer in three to four sentences, using information from the text.

expected_elements: Identifies the peculiar alignment of slopes and the horizon as the cause.
Explains that vehicles appear to roll uphill when they are not.
Connects the cause (optical illusion) to the misleading effect on visitors.
Uses at least one detail from the text's description of Magnetic Hills.

items.source_lo: Student analyses authorial language choices and rhetorical devices in an informational text using critical reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Extract 1: opening statement on mystifying phenomena; Extract 2: rhetorical question and hide-and-seek metaphor for Chandipur Beach.
items.item_stem: Read the sentence below from the text: 'Have you seen things disappearing in front of your eyes?' Which of the following best describes the writer's purpose in opening the section on Chandipur Beach with this question?

options.label: A
options.text: To compare Chandipur Beach with other disappearing natural features around the world.

options.label: B
options.text: To engage the reader's curiosity by creating a sense of mystery about what follows.

options.label: C
options.text: To indicate that the writer has personally visited Chandipur Beach.

options.label: D
options.text: To suggest that the beach is dangerous and should be approached with caution.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests a misreading of the rhetorical question as a safety warning rather than a curiosity hook.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses a rhetorical device with autobiographical narration — the question is addressed to the reader, not about the writer.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Imports a comparison frame not supported anywhere in the text's treatment of Chandipur Beach.

items.source_lo: Student analyses authorial language choices and rhetorical devices in an informational text using critical reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Extract 1: opening statement on mystifying phenomena; Extract 2: rhetorical question and hide-and-seek metaphor for Chandipur Beach.
items.item_stem: The writer describes Chandipur Beach as 'playing hide-and-seek with its visitors.' Analyse this phrase: what does it suggest about the beach's behaviour, and what effect does the writer's choice of this expression have on the reader's understanding of an otherwise scientific phenomenon?

expected_elements: Identifies 'hide-and-seek' as a metaphor comparing the tide cycle to a children's game.
Explains what the beach 'does' — sea retreats and returns, creating the illusion.
Notes that the playful language makes a tidal phenomenon feel engaging or magical.
Shows awareness that the writer balances scientific fact with figurative expression.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a spoken exchange and distinguishes accurate statements from inaccurate ones using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sibling conversation about Peru's Rainbow Mountain — mineral layers, colours, snow cover, and nature's role.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between the brother and sister about the Rainbow Mountain. Decide whether each of the following statements is True or False.
1. The sister was aware of the Rainbow Mountain before her brother mentioned it.
2. The brother did not know what caused the different colours on the mountain.
3. According to the conversation, the green colour on the mountain comes from copper minerals.
4. Both the brother and sister agreed that the mountain's colours looked fresh and bright.

options.text: According to the conversation, the green colour on the mountain comes from copper minerals.
Both the brother and sister agreed that the mountain's colours looked fresh and bright.
The brother did not know what caused the different colours on the mountain.
The sister was aware of the Rainbow Mountain before her brother mentioned it.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the sister identifies it first as her own favourite.
2. False — the brother explains the formation: mineral layers of clay, limestone, and sandstone deposited millions of years ago.
3. True — the sister states that green comes from copper.
4. False — it is the sister, not both speakers together, who comments that it looks fresh and bright after the snow melted.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a spoken exchange and distinguishes accurate statements from inaccurate ones using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sibling conversation about Peru's Rainbow Mountain — mineral layers, colours, snow cover, and nature's role.
items.item_stem: In the conversation about the Rainbow Mountain, the sister says: 'Each colour represents a different time in history.' Based on the information given in the conversation, explain in two sentences how this statement connects to what the brother said about how the mountain's colours were formed.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The brother explains that layers of minerals — clay, limestone, and sandstone — were deposited by water from ancient seas and lakes over millions of years. Because each mineral layer was laid down at a different point in geological history, each colour band on the mountain represents a distinct era, which is what the sister means by 'a different time in history.'

expected_elements: Names a specific place and gives its location clearly.
Describes one distinctive or appealing feature of the place.

items.item_stem: A friend says: 'There is no point visiting natural wonders in India when we can see them in pictures and videos.' Give your opinion on this view, with at least one reason for or against it, drawing on what you know about any of the wonders described in 'Spectacular Wonders.' Speak for about two minutes.

expected_elements: States a clear personal opinion — for or against the friend's view.
Supports the opinion with at least one specific reference to a wonder from the text.
Acknowledges the opposing view briefly before defending their own position.
Uses formal spoken register and reasons logically, not just emotionally.

items.item_stem: Write a short descriptive paragraph (eight to ten sentences) about a natural object or place you have seen — such as a river, a mountain, a forest, or a beach. Begin your paragraph with a sentence that names the place and captures what makes it striking. Use at least two descriptive details — such as colour, sound, or movement — in your paragraph.

expected_elements: Opens with a sentence naming the place and its striking quality.
Includes at least two specific sensory details (colour, sound, movement, or scale).
Paragraph is coherent and roughly eight to ten sentences.
Language is descriptive, not merely factual or list-like.

items.item_stem: Write a descriptive essay for your school magazine about a natural event or place that has left a strong impression on you. Give your essay a title. Include an introduction (one paragraph), a body (two to three paragraphs with specific details about what you saw, heard, or felt), and a conclusion that explains why this experience or place matters to you. Your essay should be approximately 250 words.

expected_elements: Essay has a title, introduction, two or three body paragraphs, and a conclusion.
Introduction establishes the subject and creates interest in the reader.
Body paragraphs use specific sensory or factual details, not vague adjectives.
Conclusion reflects on personal significance, not merely summarises.

items.item_stem: The text 'Spectacular Wonders' uses the expression 'to name a few' after listing some of the natural wonders of India. Write two sentences: one using 'to name a few' correctly, and one using the binomial 'leaps and bounds' correctly. Your sentences must be about a natural or historical topic — they should not repeat examples directly from the text.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable sample: 'The Western Ghats are home to tigers, leopards, and king cobra, to name a few.' / 'Tourism in the hill station has grown by leaps and bounds over the past decade.' Teacher should assess whether the expression is used correctly in context and whether the topic is natural or historical.

items.item_stem:
Fill in the blanks with the correct form — present participle or past participle — of the verb given in brackets.
1. The _____________ waters of Kumbalangi village attract tourists every year. (glow)
2. _____________ in basaltic rock, the Lonar Crater is considered geologically unique. (form)
3. The _____________ roots of the Meghalaya bridges take years to grow into their full shape. (intertwine)
4. The snow-_____________ peaks of the Himalayas provide a spectacular backdrop to the Valley of Flowers. (cover)

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. glowing (present participle — describes the ongoing quality of the waters). 2. Formed (past participle — describes a completed geological action, used as an adjectival phrase). 3. intertwined (past participle — describes roots in a completed state). 4. snow-covered (past participle — describes peaks in a completed state).

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies participles and gerunds in context using grammar-in-writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Participles (living, striking, rugged) and gerund (Crossing) drawn from the text; present and past participle forms; gerund vs participle distinction; sentence combining.
items.item_stem:
Read the sentences below. Rewrite each pair as a single sentence using either a gerund or a participle, as instructed.
1. Riya was amazed by the Glowing Waters. She could not stop talking about them. (Use a participle.)
2. You explore the Sundarbans by boat. It is the best way to see the tigers. (Use a gerund.)

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Amazed by the Glowing Waters, Riya could not stop talking about them. (past participle phrase at the start of the sentence). 2. Exploring the Sundarbans by boat is the best way to see the tigers. (gerund as subject of the sentence).

items.item_stem:
The text 'Spectacular Wonders' describes the Glowing Waters of Kerala as a natural phenomenon caused by micro-planktons. The firefly is another organism known for bioluminescence.

(a) What is bioluminescence?
(b) Name one way in which the bioluminescence of micro-planktons in the sea differs from that of a firefly in a field.

expected_elements: Defines bioluminescence as light produced by a living organism through a chemical process.
Notes that micro-planktons produce a collective glow visible in seawater.
Contrasts with the firefly, which produces individual, intermittent flashes in air.
Response shows awareness that both are natural, living-organism phenomena.

items.item_stem:
The text 'Spectacular Wonders' celebrates India's natural phenomena. The 'Let us explore' section points to man-made wonders such as the Kallanai Dam, the Nalanda university complex, and the musical pillars of Hampi.

Choose ONE natural wonder from the text and ONE man-made wonder from the 'Let us explore' section. Write a project note (150–200 words) comparing the two: what forces — natural or human — created each, what makes each worth preserving, and what a visitor might learn by experiencing both.

expected_elements: Names one natural wonder and one man-made wonder clearly.
Explains the force (geological, ecological, or human-engineering) that created each.
Gives at least one reason why each is worth preserving — cultural, scientific, or historical.
Connects the two by identifying what a visitor could learn from experiencing both.
